Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The study centers on introducing Fitbit fitness bands—a mainstream, utilitarian activity-tracking technology—to encourage physical activity in children with autism, addressing obesity and sedentary lifestyle. The design focus is on health/utility (increasing physical activity, technology acceptance/adoption) rather than creating or repurposing an entertainment game, and there is no description of a fun-first or game-based design process. Stakeholders (parents, therapists, researchers) are involved around a pre-existing utilitarian device, fitting a mostly utility-first approach.

        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: The core activity is children with autism wearing and using commercial Fitbit fitness bands to track physical activity. This is not free-form play or a modifiable game; it is interaction with a mainstream, rigidly rule-based tracking system (fixed feedback, step counts, app screenshots). Parents and therapists motivate use but do not change the underlying rules or structure of the technology, which best matches a game/interaction with rigid rules.

This aligns with an entirely skill/effort-based design rather than any chance-based structure.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: The study is an intervention using Fitbit fitness bands with children with autism, focusing on technology acceptance, motivation, and adoption. Use of the Fitbit (step counting, wearing the band, parental monitoring) is inherently asynchronous and not described as involving any real-time or co-temporal interaction between multiple users or systems. There is no mention of synchronous multiplayer, real-time coordination, or live feedback loops typical of synchronous or mixed systems, so the design is best characterized as entirely asynchronous.

        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),

        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The study is not a game but an observational/interview study about children with autism using Fitbit activity trackers. There are no roles, turn structures, or interactive mechanics between multiple players/participants that could create asymmetry or symmetry in a game-design sense. Since all participating children use the same type of device in the same way and there is no described role differentiation, the closest fit within the provided game-oriented scale is an entirely symmetrical structure.
